column4: The source section's literal fire-as-guide scene is explicit: Moses has seen a fire and hopes to find guidance at it (هُدًى); this joins its نَارٌ to a coal, a traveler, and a guide in one moment.
This ayah gives the section's night-travel function to the stars: they are made as guides through the darknesses of land and sea, much as the distant fire lets a traveler correct direction.
The ayah pairs road markers (عَلَامَات) with finding direction by a star, a close counterpart to the source section's menār, a sign on the road, and its night-sky guidance.

This ayah lays out paths through the land so people may find their way; the next ayah, 16:16, adds markers and the star that orient them, completing this row's road with the source section's sign-fire image.

Moses sees a fire and may bring a glowing brand so his family can warm themselves; the source section explicitly sets this reachable, warming fire beside 92:15's ص ل ي root for entering and burning in the other fire.

Moses sees fire at the mountain's side while traveling with his family. The source section identifies “side” (جَانِب) as the dictionary root ج ن ب also heard in 92:17's being kept away, setting approach to this fire against distance from the blazing one.
Lot is told to travel with his family at night, follow their rear, and let no one look back; this supplies the source section's exact rearguard position and forward-only travel.
God commands Moses to travel by night and makes a dry path through the sea for his people; it joins a guided night journey to a route opened for a traveling group.

Pharaoh goes ahead of his people and brings them to the Fire. This reverses the source section's guide at the head of a caravan and fire as a warning sign: a leader can take the whole procession to the danger itself.
These leaders invite people to the Fire, a direct reversal of a guide who uses fire to show travelers where the road lies and where it ends.

This ayah says the Hereafter and the first life belong to God, repeating the source section's paired “last and first” order (الآخرة والأولى) and extending its caravan's head-to-tail span to God's sovereignty over both lives.
God makes roads in the earth so people may be guided; the source section defines هداية as making roads known and imagines a sign that lets the traveler find one.

Its lamp and layered light end with God guiding whom He wills to His light; that makes the source section's dictionary link between نُور and نَار through illumination concrete as a symbol that guides.
The ayah calls revelation a light by which God guides people to a straight path; it joins the source section's linked نور/نار illumination, guidance, and the road the traveler needs to find.
A light and a clear Book guide people to paths of peace; the verse concretely brings together the source section's نور/نار illumination note, hidaya, and roads.
The ayah describes giving for God's sake as seeking His Face (ابْتِغَاءَ وَجْهِ اللَّهِ), closely matching the source section's Face as the walker's aim.
These servants seek their Lord's Face and spend from what God provided; the pairing of Face-seeking and giving mirrors the source section's destination for the generous walk.
The speakers say they feed others only for the Face of God (لِوَجْهِ اللَّهِ), a direct parallel to the source section's Face as the intention that directs one's path.
This second telling of Lot's escape repeats the night departure and no-look-back command, adding that his wife is the exception; it sharpens the boundary between continuing forward and turning back.

Night and day are made as signs, with night darkened and day made visible so people can seek provision and reckon time; this explains the source section's contrast between a path visible by day and needing a fire by night.
The ayah assigns night to rest and day to seeing (مُبْصِرًا), giving the source section's night-and-day travel distinction its practical contrast in visibility.
Daylight's disclosure in this oath directly echoes the source section's day appearing into broad light, when travelers need no guiding fire.
Night's covering in this paired oath directly echoes the source section's darkened road, when the distant fire becomes a guide.
The ayah describes night and day wrapping over one another, extending the source section's alternating covered night and disclosed day into a recurring cycle.
The revealed Book brings people from darkness to light and to the path of the Mighty; this gives the source section's night-and-guiding-light image a scriptural path between darkness and disclosure.
Moses is sent to bring his people from darkness into light, joining the same prophet who sees a night fire in the source section to guidance out of darkness.
The ayah gives a person light “by which he walks among people” (يَمْشِي بِهِ فِي النَّاسِ), a walking-light counterpart to the traveler who sees a distant fire and sets his direction.

God gives believers a light “by which you walk” (تَمْشُونَ بِهِ); this directly extends the source section's traveler whose path is made visible by an external fire into guidance carried along the way.
At judgment, believers' light runs before them and at their right; light placed ahead of a moving group develops the source section's image of a guide visible in front.
Believers again have light running before them and on their right as they ask God to complete it; this repeated judgment scene makes light a forward guide for travelers toward their destination.
The ayah says the straight road is God's to point out, while some ways turn aside; it develops the source section's hidaya as identifying a road and the warning fire as marking a boundary.
God guides the human being to the two paths (النَّجْدَيْنِ); the fork makes the source section's guide and warning fire a choice of direction rather than a general religious theme.
The way is shown to the human being, who may respond gratefully or reject it; this makes explicit the traveler's response to guidance that the source section's road-sign image implies.
God calls to the Home of Peace and guides whom He wills to a straight path, giving the source section's road-guiding image a defined destination as well as direction.

This ayah pictures a bewildered traveler on earth whose companions call him toward guidance while devils pull him away; its competing directions clarify why the source section's traveler must recognize and follow a true sign.
God makes prophets leaders guiding by His command; that group being led develops the source section's hadī as the guide who goes ahead of a following caravan.
God makes leaders who guide by His command, again giving the source section's hidaya a human guide at the front of a community.
Those who strive for God are promised guidance to His ways; this links the source section's seeker of the Lord's Face to the paths that guidance makes known.
The ayah says that wherever people turn, there is God's Face; its explicit turning and orientation give spatial force to the source section's dictionary sense of وَجْه as the place one faces.
The command to set one's face toward the upright religion uses وَجْه as bodily orientation, matching the source section's image of walking with the Lord's Face as one's direction.

The source section uses first/last for both a caravan's ends and the two lives; this ayah applies al-Awwal and al-Akhir to God Himself, shifting that same pair from a created sequence to divine scope.
The ayah names one who turns away from God's remembrance and seeks only the nearer life; it gives a concrete counter-direction to the source section's traveler moving toward the Lord's Face.
The source section points out the denier's turn-away action; this ayah uses the same turning-away verb after a man considers the reminder, opposing a traveler who stays oriented toward guidance.

Moses reaches the fire and is called by name; this immediate continuation of 20:10 answers the source section's possibility of finding guidance at a fire by making it the place where divine guidance begins.
At the fire Moses hears a call and its surroundings are declared blessed; this continuation of 27:7 turns the expected warmth or report into a meeting with the source of guidance.

After Moses sees the fire at the mountain's side in 28:29, this ayah places the call from the valley's right side and a blessed spot; it completes the source section's side/fire encounter with a voice that gives direction.
Hell is seen from a distant place; this reverses the source section's traveler seeing a far fire as a useful guide, since here the far-seen fire is itself the threatening destination.

Pharaoh tells his people to follow him, claiming to guide them to the right way; unlike the source section's hādī, the guide who goes ahead, 11:98 reveals where this leader actually brings his people.
Night is made a covering, giving another direct formulation of the source section's darkened travel scene in which a fire is needed to disclose the road.
Day is made for livelihood, adding a repeated Quranic night/day division to the source section's contrast between night travel and the broad visibility of day.
God makes night and day for rest and the pursuit of bounty; this gives the source section's two travel modes a repeated Quranic account of their different uses.
Sleep at night and seeking bounty by day are signs; this repeats the source section's distinction between a night walker and one who can travel in daylight.
Night and day succeed one another as a reminder; this adds the recurring alternation that underlies the source section's paired orders of night and day.
Abraham says he has turned his face toward the Creator of the heavens and earth; the source section's dictionary sense of وَجْه as what one faces is bodily orientation here, directed toward God.
These callers worship their Lord morning and evening while seeking His Face; the source section's Face-seeking walker meets a group whose daily devotion is oriented toward the same divine aim.
The ayah describes people who call on their Lord morning and evening seeking His Face; their steady orientation to God extends the source section's Face as the walker's destination.
The ayah invites whoever wills to take a way to his Lord; it makes explicit the path-to-the-Lord relation that the source section develops from seeking the Lord's Face.
This repeated formulation again offers a way to the Lord, clarifying that the source section's Face-seeking image has a destination as well as a direction.

God identifies His straight path and commands people to follow it, warning against other paths that divide them from it; this makes the source section's road-sign image a choice between staying on a route and straying.
